title: Merge overlapping guesthouse bookings
prompt:
A guesthouse stores each booking as a room plus the first and last night stayed (both inclusive). Bookings for the same room can overlap after double-booking mistakes, and some sit back to back.

The cleaning rota needs continuous occupied blocks per room. Merge a room's bookings when they overlap or when one starts the night right after another block ends (first_night = block end + 1 day).

- Columns: room, block_start, block_end, bookings
- Any row order is fine
- bookings is how many booking rows were merged into the block
- A single free night between bookings keeps them in separate blocks
hints: Sort each room's bookings by first_night. A booking starts a new block when it begins after everything before it has ended (plus one night).
Comparing with only the previous booking's last_night fails when an earlier long booking covers later short ones. Use the running maximum of last_night over all earlier rows.

max(last_night) OVER (PARTITION BY room ORDER BY first_night, last_night, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) gives prev_end. Flag first_night > prev_end + 1 (or NULL prev_end) as 1, running-sum the flags into a block id, then group.

exercise.starter:
-- Occupied blocks per room
-- (each booking is its own block for now)
SELECT room,
       first_night AS block_start,
       last_night AS block_end,
       1 AS bookings
FROM room_bookings;
exercise.solution:
WITH o AS (
  SELECT id, room, first_night, last_night,
         max(last_night) OVER (
           PARTITION BY room ORDER BY first_night, last_night, id
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
         ) AS prev_end
  FROM room_bookings
), f AS (
  SELECT *,
         CASE WHEN prev_end IS NULL OR first_night > prev_end + 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new
  FROM o
), g AS (
  SELECT *,
         sum(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY room ORDER BY first_night, last_night, id) AS block_id
  FROM f
)
SELECT room,
       min(first_night) AS block_start,
       max(last_night) AS block_end,
       count(*) AS bookings
FROM g
GROUP BY room, block_id;

tests.name: back to back merges per room

hiddenTests.name: long booking contains later short ones
one free night keeps blocks apart
month boundary and same nights in other rooms

explanation: Sorted by first_night, a booking belongs to the current block exactly when it starts no later than one night after the furthest last_night seen so far in that room. The running max over earlier rows (excluding the current one) captures that furthest end; a running sum of 'starts a new block' flags then numbers the blocks, and grouping by it collapses each block. The trap is lag(last_night): a long booking that swallows several short ones is forgotten after one row, so the 10th–12th booking would wrongly start a new block. The + 1 handles back-to-back stays, and adding id to the ORDER BY makes the frame deterministic when bookings start on the same night.
notes: Both windows share the same PARTITION BY and ORDER BY, so Postgres sorts once and evaluates them in sequence; an index on (room, first_night) can remove that sort. Postgres also offers range types and the range_agg aggregate, which merges overlapping ranges directly, e.g. range_agg(daterange(first_night, last_night, '[]')) per room; daterange canonicalises to [) so adjacent stays merge too, but you lose the per-block booking count. An exclusion constraint (EXCLUDE USING gist with btree_gist) would prevent the double bookings in the first place.
followUps: Solve it with range_agg and unnest. What does the result look like, and what do you lose?
How would you prevent overlapping bookings for the same room at write time?
